title: A tea bag and a sieve: three ways across the membrane
placement: Module 13, section `physiology` (Convection, replacement fluid, and the filtration fraction); analogy introduced in `model` (A sieve as well as a tea bag)
job: U — the learner can see why convection removes middle molecules that diffusion leaves behind, and what the sieving coefficient means.
skill: williamriveromd-biomedical-mechanism-figure (+ circuit-skill filter rules: blood in at the bottom, out at the top)
alt: Diffusion, ultrafiltration, and convection across a filter fiber wall, with sieving coefficients near one for urea, lower for larger molecules, near zero for albumin.
caption: Diffusion moves small solutes down a concentration difference; convection drags solutes of any size up to the pore limit along with water pushed through by pressure. Each solute's sieving coefficient says how freely it crosses.
reviewer_flags: The text gives "lower for larger molecules" and names beta-2 microglobulin as the example of a larger molecule cleared poorly by diffusion; the figure places beta-2 microglobulin in the "lower" band without a number. Confirm that wording. No numeric sieving coefficient is shown other than the text's "close to 1" and "close to 0".

title: Pre-dilution or post-dilution, and the filtration fraction
placement: Module 13, section `physiology` (Convection, replacement fluid, and the filtration fraction)
job: U/A — the learner can predict how the replacement-fluid site changes clearance and filter life, and can work the filtration fraction from blood flow and hematocrit.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold B comparison with a worked-example strip; circuit-skill port rules for the two mini filters)
alt: Pre-dilution versus post-dilution replacement fluid compared, with the worked filtration fraction: 35 mL/min removed from 140 mL/min plasma flow equals 25%.
caption: Replacement fluid given before the filter keeps blood thinner and the filter alive longer, at some cost in clearance; given after, every liter removed is the patient's own plasma water, but blood thickens in the fibers. The filtration fraction measures how hard the filter is working.
reviewer_flags: The 25% in the worked example is the text's illustrative arithmetic, not a ceiling; the figure labels it "worked example" and states that the ceiling is set by unit protocol. Confirm. No percentage clearance loss for pre-dilution is shown (the circuit skill's "about 15%" is not in the module and was removed).

title: The four continuous modes, and SLED
placement: Module 13, section `crrt-modes` (The four continuous modes, and the prolonged intermittent alternative)
job: U — the learner can name which pumps and fluids run in each mode, by which mechanism it clears, and why it is chosen.
alt: Reference card comparing SCUF, CVVH, CVVHD, and CVVHDF by fluids used, mechanism, what each removes best, and why chosen, with SLED as the prolonged alternative.
caption: The name of the mode tells you which pumps are running, and therefore which fluids, bags, and checks apply. Every mode can also remove fluid, and no mode has proven survival benefit over another.
reviewer_flags: "Roughly 6 to 12 hours" for SLED is flagged in m13_x.py FLAGS as a general-practice description without a single cited source; it appears here verbatim. Confirm.

title: CVVHDF circuit with regional citrate and calcium
placement: Module 13, section `crrt-anticoag` (Keeping the circuit open: no anticoagulant, heparin, or regional citrate); also supports `crrt-circuit` (The circuit: priming, pressures, filter life, and alarms)
job: U — the learner can trace blood, dialysate, replacement fluid, citrate, and calcium through a CVVHDF circuit and say where each pressure and sample is taken.
skill: dialysis-circuit-schematic (locked topology; modality CVVHDF: countercurrent dialysate PLUS replacement)
alt: CVVHDF circuit from a jugular dialysis catheter: citrate enters the red access line, dialysate runs countercurrent, replacement fluid joins one blood line, calcium returns separately.
caption: Citrate enters the blood line just after it leaves the patient and binds calcium so the circuit cannot clot; much of it leaves in the effluent, and calcium is replaced into the patient by a separate infusion. Dialysate runs outside the fibers against the blood; replacement fluid joins the blood line itself.
reviewer_flags: (1) Calcium site: the text allows the return line OR a separate central line; the figure draws a separate purple line to a separate central venous line, labeled "per protocol", and notes the alternative. Confirm. (2) Citrate site: the text says "just after it leaves the patient"; the figure places the citrate tee on the red line after the access-pressure point and before the blood pump (simple-figure skill order). Confirm against the ICU's machine. (3) Post-filter sample site placed on the blue line between the filter outlet and the post-dilution tee; the text says only "from the circuit after the filter". Confirm. (4) Removed from the circuit-skill template because the module does not state them: KDIGO dose 20–25 mL/kg/h on the circuit, "about 15%" pre-dilution clearance loss, filtration fraction 20–25%, IHD 500 mL/min, five-modality legend, and blood pump "mL/min" label. (5) Catheter in the right internal jugular with the tip at the SVC–right atrial junction is a circuit-skill anatomy rule; the module says only "non-tunneled dialysis central venous catheter". (6) Amber #C9A84C (citrate) and purple #4B3280 (calcium) are additions to the circuit palette, declared in the legend.

title: Three fluid numbers that must agree
placement: Module 13, section `crrt-fluid` (Hourly fluid balance: three numbers that must agree); also supports `bedside` (Safety rules shared by every convective therapy)
job: A — the learner can reconcile the machine's net removal with the patient's total balance and the prescribed goal, and knows when to call.
skill: williamriveromd-simple-figure (Scaffold E reference card with a worked-hour strip)
alt: Machine net removal, patient total balance, and prescribed goal compared, with a worked hour where the machine removes 250 mL yet the patient is 50 mL short.
caption: The machine counts only its own fluids; it knows nothing about the infusions, the feed, or the urine bag. Record all three numbers every hour and report when they drift apart or the patient cannot tolerate removal.
reviewer_flags: none (all values are the text's illustrative arithmetic; the drift limit is "the protocol's limit" with no number).

title: Circuit alarms: patient first, then the circuit
placement: Module 13, section `crrt-circuit` (The circuit: priming, pressures, filter life, and alarms)
job: A — the learner can match each continuous-therapy alarm or trend to its likely cause, take the first nursing check, and escalate, without ever overriding air detection.
alt: Continuous therapy alarm algorithm: access, return, pre-filter and transmembrane trends, air and blood leak alarms, each mapped to likely cause, first check, and escalation.
caption: Look at the patient before the machine. Rising transmembrane pressure or pressure drop predicts clotting hours ahead, which gives time to report and plan a change with blood return; air and blood-leak detectors are never overridden.

title: What continuous clearance takes away: the watch table
placement: Module 13, section `crrt-complications` (Complications, and what continuous clearance takes away)

alt: Watch table for continuous therapy: hypothermia, electrolyte losses, acid–base, bleeding, catheter problems, drug removal, nutrition, low platelets, each with signs and action.

title: Online HDF: the machine makes its own infusion fluid
placement: Module 13 page, section `hdf-principles` (Online hemodiafiltration: how the machine makes fluid safe to infuse)
job: U — the learner sees how treated water becomes ultrapure dialysate and then sterile substitution fluid that joins the blood line after the dialyzer, and what convection adds.
skill: williamriveromd-biomedical-mechanism-figure, with dialysis-circuit-schematic port rules (end caps blood only, side ports fluid only, substitution joins the blood line)
alt: Online HDF fluid path: treated water and concentrates become dialysate, pass two ultrafilters, and enter the venous blood line after a high-flux dialyzer.
caption: In online HDF the machine filters its own dialysate twice: once to make ultrapure dialysate for the dialyzer, and again to make sterile substitution fluid that runs straight into the blood. That is why the substitution line is handled like an intravenous line.
reviewer_flags: (1) Resolved: the lesson now gives beta-2 microglobulin as about 11,800 daltons throughout; this figure still omits the number. (2) The circuit is simplified: no pressure monitors, air detector or anticoagulant line are drawn, because this figure teaches the fluid path. A reviewer may want the air detector added on the venous line between the substitution junction and the patient. (3) Dialysate enters at the upper side port, countercurrent; the HDF text does not say which way the dialysate flows, so this comes from the house circuit rule.

title: Convection volume: the arithmetic that decides the dose
placement: Module 13 page, section `hdf-prescription` (The HDF prescription: convection volume and what drives it)
job: A — the learner adds substitution and net UF volumes and sees how a lower blood flow or a shortened session misses the target.
alt: Convection volume equals substitution plus net ultrafiltration; worked example shows how lower blood flow or a shorter session drops 23 liters to 19.4 or 17.8.
caption: Convection volume is everything filtered across the membrane: the substitution volume plus the net ultrafiltration. With the same fraction of blood flow, a weaker access or a shorter session misses the target even though the substitution setting never changed.

title: The HDF trials at a glance
placement: Module 13 page, section `hdf-evidence` (What the trials show, and what they do not)
job: U/P — the learner sees why early trials looked neutral, why CONVINCE was different, and which findings are associations.
alt: Six HDF studies compared: CONTRAST, Turkish, ESHOL, CONVINCE, and two pooled analyses, with patients, comparator, and result; volume link shown as association.
caption: The trials that delivered lower convection volumes found no overall survival difference; CONVINCE randomized only patients able to receive high volumes and found lower mortality. The link between higher achieved volume and better survival is an association, not proof.
reviewer_flags: (1) Dense: six rows × four columns plus a footer band. If the hazard ratios or intervals come back garbled after two tries, use an HTML table (the page already has this table in HTML) and keep the image to the "Why results differed" band only. (2) The ESHOL comparator is "continued HD" (the text does not say low-flux or high-flux); the figure keeps that wording. (3) Pooled 2016 has no hazard ratio in the text, so only the percentages are shown.

title: HDF alarms: meaning, first check, escalate
placement: Module 13 page, section `hdf-session` (Running an HDF session: before, during, and after), beside the alarm table
job: A — the learner matches each HDF-specific alarm to its likely meaning, first nursing check, and the point at which to escalate.
alt: Algorithm for six HDF alarms: transmembrane pressure, substitution fault, blood leak, conductivity, filtration fraction limit, failed ultrafilter test, with first checks and escalation.
caption: Find the cause before resetting any alarm, and never widen a limit to keep the session running. A blood leak or a failed ultrafilter test always goes to the charge nurse and the physician or technician.
reviewer_flags: (1) The plan listed five alarms; the module table has six, so the ultrafilter integrity test is included. (2) The rigor banner comes from the "Temperature" bullet of `hdf-session`, not the alarm table. (3) Limits and permitted substitution-rate changes depend on the machine and protocol (module quiz flag); the figure shows reasoning only.
